reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: Inflammation of the external auditory canal presenting with ear pain, itching, discharge and a feeling of fullness
Pain on moving the tragus or pinna is a hallmark that helps distinguish it from middle ear disease
Moisture, trauma from cotton buds, and a disrupted acidic canal environment are common predisposing factors
The localised furuncular form is a staphylococcal infection of a hair follicle in the outer cartilaginous canal, while the diffuse form is often associated with Pseudomonas
Otomycosis (fungal otitis externa) typically shows itching with visible fungal debris such as blotting-paper or fluffy growth in the canal
Management principles include meticulous aural toileting, topical antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory drops, analgesia and keeping the ear dry
Malignant (necrotising) otitis externa is a serious osteomyelitis of the skull base, seen mainly in elderly diabetics and the immunocompromised, and demands urgent recognition
Recurrent or treatment-resistant disease should prompt review for underlying dermatological conditions, diabetes or immunosuppression
reference.pathophysiology: Otitis externa is inflammation of the skin lining the external auditory canal. Breakdown of the canal's protective barrier, through excess moisture, mechanical trauma, cerumen removal, or altered pH, allows bacterial or fungal overgrowth. The resulting inflammation causes oedema, discharge and narrowing of the canal, producing pain and conductive hearing loss when the lumen is occluded. In malignant otitis externa, infection (typically Pseudomonas) spreads from the soft tissue into the temporal bone and skull base, causing progressive osteomyelitis and potential cranial nerve involvement.
additionalDifferentials: Acute otitis media with perforation and discharge
Eczematous or seborrhoeic dermatitis of the canal
additionalInvestigations: Otoscopy or otomicroscopy to inspect the canal and clear debris
Swab of discharge for bacterial and fungal culture in resistant cases
Blood glucose and inflammatory markers when necrotising disease is suspected
CT or MRI of the temporal bone and skull base for suspected malignant otitis externa
Biopsy of granulation tissue where malignancy or necrotising disease is a concern
redFlags: Severe, disproportionate pain with granulation tissue in an elderly diabetic suggesting necrotising otitis externa
Cranial nerve palsies (especially facial nerve) indicating skull base osteomyelitis
Spreading cellulitis, fever or systemic upset
Failure to respond to standard topical therapy
reference.prognosis: Uncomplicated otitis externa usually resolves with topical treatment and ear care, but malignant otitis externa is potentially life-threatening and requires prolonged systemic therapy and close monitoring.
pitfalls: Missing a perforation or middle ear disease as the source of discharge
Overlooking necrotising otitis externa in a diabetic with severe pain
Ineffective treatment because the canal was not adequately cleaned
Failing to identify and treat an underlying fungal or dermatological cause
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Meticulous aural toilet to clear debris and allow topical therapy to reach the canal skin
Topical antibiotic and corticosteroid ear drops, with an ear wick inserted when the canal is oedematous and occluded
Adequate analgesia with advice to keep the ear dry and avoid cotton buds or further trauma
Incision or drainage of a localised furuncle in the cartilaginous canal where it points
Antifungal drops for otomycosis identified on otoscopy after thorough debris removal
Urgent recognition of malignant (necrotising) otitis externa, with systemic anti-pseudomonal antibiotics, skull-base imaging and specialist ENT referral
Correct predisposing factors such as moisture exposure and address diabetes or immunosuppression
